summary: This document describes how a service provider can offer IPv6 VPN service over its packet-switched backbone by extending BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. It defines an IPv6 VPN address family and its route distribution in Multiprotocol BGP, working over IPv4 or IPv6 backbones and tunnels such as MPLS, IP-in-IP, GRE and IPsec.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC shows how a service provider can offer private networks to customers who use IPv6, using the same design it already uses for IPv4. Each customer network keeps its own IPv6 addresses, and a number in front of the address tells the provider which network it belongs to.

questions: how do ipv6 vpns work over mpls
what is bgp mpls ipv6 vpn
subtitle: How a service provider carries IPv6 private networks over its own packet backbone.

tldr.problem: A service provider that sells private networks to its customers over an IP backbone had a method for IPv4, but nothing that carried IPv6 sites in the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the BGP/MPLS IP VPN method of RFC 4364 with one addition: a VPN-IPv6 address family, in which a route distinguisher is placed in front of the IPv6 address, so each VPN can keep its own address space.
tldr.outcome: An IPv6 VPN runs over an IPv4 or an IPv6 backbone with the same procedures, the same tunnels and the same management as an IPv4 VPN, and the service looks the same to the customer either way.

facts.label: Next Hop length, global address only

today: RFC 4659 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends the BGP/MPLS IP VPN method of RFC 4364, which remains the base it builds on.

sections.title: The Method in One Page
sections.content:
The document describes how a service provider can use its packet-switched backbone to provide virtual private network services for its IPv6 customers. It reuses and extends the BGP/MPLS IP VPN method of RFC 4364, and in particular uses the same peer model: the customer's edge routers, the CE routers, send their IPv6 routes to the provider's edge routers, the PE routers. BGP is then used by the provider to exchange the routes of one IPv6 VPN among the PE routers attached to that VPN, and those PE routers pass the IPv6 routes on to the CE routers of that VPN. As in IPv4, the CE routers of a VPN do not peer with each other, so there is no overlay visible to the VPN's own routing algorithm.

Unless the document says otherwise, it adopts the definitions, acronyms and mechanisms of RFC 4364 without repeating them. A VPN is an IPv6 VPN when each of its sites is IPv6 capable and connected natively over an IPv6 interface or sub-interface to the provider backbone through a provider edge device. A site may be both IPv4 capable and IPv6 capable: the logical interface on which packets arrive at the provider edge may decide the IP version, or, when one interface carries both, the version field of the IP header decides it packet by packet.

The scope is narrow on purpose. Only IPv6 traffic between IPv6 hosts on IPv6-capable sites is covered. Handling IPv4 traffic between IPv4 hosts is covered by RFC 4364, and traffic between an IPv4 host and an IPv6 host is outside the scope of this document. Like the IPv4 method, each IPv6 VPN may have its own address space, so the same address can denote different systems in different VPNs. That is achieved with a new address family, the VPN-IPv6 address family, which prepends a route distinguisher to the IP address in the same way as the VPN-IPv4 address family of RFC 4364.

Where the IPv4 solution runs over MPLS label switched paths, this document also allows the IPv6 VPN to run over other tunnels, including GRE, IP-in-IP, L2TPv3 and IPsec protected tunnels. The service works over an IPv4 backbone and over an IPv6 backbone, and the service supported is the same in both cases.

The document lists four benefits: from the provider's point of view and from the customer's, the IPv6 VPN service is identical to the IPv4 one; operating it needs the same skills, procedures and mechanisms; where both are offered over an IPv4 core, the same multiprotocol BGP peering relationships and the same provider-to-provider tunnel mesh can be used for both; and the service does not depend on whether the core runs IPv4 or IPv6, so a customer cannot tell whether the core has been migrated. Supporting IPv4 VPN services over an IPv6 core is not covered.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider's method for IPv4 private networks is extended to IPv6. The customer router hands its IPv6 routes to the provider, the provider tells the other provider routers attached to the same private network about those routes, and those routers pass them to the other customer routers. The customer routers never talk to each other directly, so the private network is invisible to their own routing.

sections.title: The VPN-IPv6 Address Family
sections.content:
The multiprotocol extensions to BGP let BGP carry routes from several address families. This document adds the VPN-IPv6 address family, which works like the VPN-IPv4 address family of RFC 4364. A VPN-IPv6 address is a 24-octet quantity: it begins with an 8-octet route distinguisher and ends with a 16-octet IPv6 address.

The route distinguisher exists for one reason, to allow distinct routes to a common IPv6 address prefix. As in RFC 4364, two different VPN-IPv6 routes can carry the same IPv6 part with different route distinguishers, which lets the provider's BGP install several different routes to the same system and lets policy decide which packets use which route. The same mechanism keeps two VPNs apart: if two VPNs use the same IPv6 prefix for different physical systems, the provider edge devices turn them into unique VPN-IPv6 prefixes with different route distinguishers, so the same address can have two completely different routes, one per VPN.

Because VPN-IPv6 addresses and IPv6 addresses belong to different address families, BGP never treats them as comparable addresses. A VRF may hold several equal-cost VPN-IPv6 routes for one IPv6 prefix, and when a packet's destination address is matched in a VRF against a VPN-IPv6 route, only the IPv6 part is actually matched. The format and encoding of the route distinguisher are as specified in RFC 4364.

Where a site is both IPv4 capable and IPv6 capable, the same route distinguisher may be used to advertise the IPv6 and the IPv4 addresses, or different ones may be used. Either way, IPv4 addresses and IPv6 addresses are always handled in separate contexts, and the document does not discuss IPv4 to IPv6 interworking.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route in the private network is written as a route distinguisher followed by the IPv6 address. The route distinguisher says which private network the address belongs to, so the same IPv6 address can mean different things in different private networks. When a packet is looked up, only the IPv6 part is compared.

sections.title: How the Routes Reach the Other Provider Routers
sections.content:
If two sites of a VPN attach to provider edge routers in the same autonomous system, those routers can distribute the VPN routes to each other over an internal BGP connection. Alternatively, each provider edge router can hold an internal BGP connection to a route reflector, which relays the routes on behalf of the others. For an IPv6 VPN the internal BGP connections may run over IPv4 or over IPv6.

The provider edge routers exchange reachability information for the IPv6 prefixes of their IPv6 VPNs through the multiprotocol extensions to BGP, and in doing so they announce themselves as the BGP next hop. The rules for encoding that reachability information, and the address of the next hop itself, are given in the following sections.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider routers pass the routes to each other over internal BGP, either directly or through a route reflector that relays them. The same session may run over IPv4 or IPv6, and the route that is sent says which provider router the traffic should be forwarded to.

sections.title: How the Route Is Encoded
sections.content:
When the provider edge router distributes IPv6 VPN routes, it must assign and distribute MPLS labels with them. In effect the routers do not distribute plain IPv6 VPN routes but labelled IPv6 VPN routes. When the advertising router later receives a packet carrying the label it advertised, it pops that label from the MPLS stack and processes the packet, either forwarding it directly according to the label or looking it up in the matching IPv6 VPN context.

The multiprotocol extensions carry the routes in the MP_REACH network layer reachability information field. Two fields there must be set: the Address Family Identifier must be 2, which is IPv6, and the Subsequent Address Family Identifier must be 128, which is MPLS labelled VPN-IPv6. The reachability information itself is encoded as specified in RFC 3107, so in this case the prefix is an 8-octet route distinguisher followed by an IPv6 prefix, as described above.

The document notes that both code points are already in the IANA registries: AFI 2 is registered for IPv6, and SAFI 128 is registered for MPLS-labelled VPN addresses. No new allocation is needed for this document. Two provider edge routers must also use the BGP capability negotiation to confirm that both can process these routes, using capability code 1 for multiprotocol BGP with the AFI and SAFI values above.
sections.plainLanguage: The route is sent with an MPLS label attached, so the receiving provider router can forward the traffic without looking the address up again. Two numbers identify the format: 2 for IPv6 and 128 for labelled VPN addresses. Both routers check that they understand the format before exchanging routes.

sections.title: The Next Hop Address and the Address Types
sections.content:
The encoding of the BGP next hop depends on whether the router wants the traffic to reach it over IPv6 tunnelling or over IPv4 tunnelling. Choosing that policy is the network operator's job and is outside the scope of the document, and it is possible to ask for IPv4 tunnelling while the BGP speakers exchange IPv6 reachability over IPv6, or the other way round. The document warns about that combination: a fault on the tunnelling data path that does not affect the reachability path can go unnoticed by BGP, and the result is traffic being dropped without explanation.

When IPv6 tunnelling is requested, the router must advertise a next hop address made of a VPN-IPv6 address whose 8-octet route distinguisher is set to zero and whose 16-octet IPv6 address is the global IPv6 address of the advertising router. This may be followed by a second VPN-IPv6 address, again with a route distinguisher of zero, holding the link-local IPv6 address of the advertising router. The length of the next hop field is 24 when only the global address is present and 48 when a link-local address is included as well. If the two speakers peer using only their link-local addresses, the advertising router uses the unspecified address to say that no global address is present. The link-local address must be included if and only if the advertising router shares a common subnet with the peer it is advertising to, and in all other cases only the global address is advertised. A router advertising to an internal peer may remove the link-local address from the field. One case where both addresses are advertised is a multi-autonomous-system backbone where border routers in different autonomous systems share a common IPv6 subnet.

When IPv4 tunnelling is requested, the router must advertise a VPN-IPv6 address whose route distinguisher is zero and whose 16-octet IPv6 address is an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address holding the IPv4 address of the advertising router. That IPv4 address must be routable by the other BGP speaker.

The document also says which kinds of IPv6 address the service carries. Link-local unicast addresses are for one link only, so they may be used on the link between the provider edge and the customer edge but are not supported across sites and are never advertised to remote provider routers. Global unicast addresses are supported across sites and are advertised, and are processed without special treatment for their global scope. Unique local IPv6 unicast addresses are supported across sites as well, because RFC 4193 says they can be used for inter-site VPNs when the routes are in place, and because they keep working if the sites are renumbered or merged; they may be advertised to remote provider routers and are processed the same way as global addresses. Which type to use in a given environment is left to the operator.
sections.plainLanguage: The route says which provider router the traffic should go to next, and the address in that field also says how to reach it. If the provider wants IPv6 tunnels, the address is a normal IPv6 address, with a link-local address added when both routers are on the same subnet. If it wants IPv4 tunnels, the IPv4 address is written in the IPv6 field in its mapped form.

sections.title: How a Packet Is Carried Across the Backbone
sections.content:
The ingress provider edge router must tunnel the IPv6 VPN data over the backbone towards the egress provider edge router named as the BGP next hop for the destination prefix. When the IPv6 address in the next hop field is an IPv4-mapped address, the ingress router must use IPv4 tunnelling unless it has been configured explicitly to do otherwise, and it may be configured to allow IPv6 tunnelling in that case. When the address is not IPv4-mapped, the ingress router must use IPv6 tunnelling.

The forwarding path itself follows the ordinary steps. A provider edge router that receives a packet from an attached customer edge router looks up the packet's IPv6 destination address in the VRF that belongs to that customer, which yields a VPN-IPv6 route with an associated MPLS label and an associated BGP next hop. The label is pushed on the packet as the bottom label, and the labelled packet is then encapsulated into the tunnel that leads to the egress router.

Which tunnel that is depends on the technique in use. With IPv4 or IPv6 tunnels, and with IPv4 or IPv6 GRE tunnels, the result is an MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE packet as specified in RFC 4023. With L2TPv3, the result is an MPLS-in-L2TPv3 packet. With an IPsec protected tunnel, the result is again MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE, and IPsec transport mode secures the tunnel from the ingress router to the egress router. When IPv4 tunnels are used, the ingress router must use the IPv4 address from the IPv4-mapped next hop field as the destination of the prepended IPv4 header, and one of its own IPv4 addresses as the source. The same rule applies with IPv6 tunnels and the IPv6 address in the next hop field.

With MPLS label switched paths, the paths may be set up with any label distribution technique, such as LDP or RSVP-TE. In that case the ingress router must push the tunnel label directly on the label stack of the labelled packet, with no IPv4 or IPv6 header in front of it. The next hop field identifies the egress router and therefore the label to push; when the address in the next hop field is IPv4-mapped, the embedded IPv4 address determines the tunnel label, and otherwise the IPv6 address does. So that systems can interoperate, every implementation of this architecture must support tunnelling over MPLS label switched paths set up with LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The router that receives a packet looks up the destination in the table for that customer, pushes the label the route carries, and puts the packet in a tunnel to the router that advertised it. The tunnel may be an MPLS path, a GRE tunnel, an L2TPv3 tunnel or an IPsec protected tunnel, and the choice of how the headers are stacked follows the technique used.

sections.title: Bigger Networks and Other Cases
sections.content:
When two sites of an IPv6 VPN attach to provider edge routers in different autonomous systems, the document applies the three procedures of RFC 4364, which have the same scalability properties, with some additions. Approach (a) connects the VRFs of the two border routers. The border routers exchange plain IPv6 routes rather than VPN-IPv6 routes, and may peer over IPv6 or over IPv4; the exchange must follow RFC 2545. This approach uses no label switched paths between the autonomous systems. Because each autonomous system implements the intra-domain procedures on its own, some autonomous systems may use IPv4 tunnelling internally while others use IPv6 tunnelling.

Approach (b) redistributes labelled VPN-IPv6 routes from one autonomous system to a neighbouring one with external BGP. The exchange of labelled VPN-IPv6 routes must follow RFC 2545 and RFC 3107. When the traffic is to be carried with IPv6 tunnelling, the next hop field must hold an IPv6 address, and when it is to be carried with IPv4 tunnelling, it must hold an IPv4 address written as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. This approach requires label switched paths between the autonomous systems, so the security considerations that RFC 4364 states for its equivalent procedure apply here as well. Again, the autonomous systems may differ in the tunnelling they use internally.

Approach (c) redistributes labelled VPN-IPv6 routes between the source and destination autonomous systems with multihop external BGP, while labelled IPv4 or IPv6 routes are redistributed from one autonomous system to the next. All the participating autonomous systems must use the same tunnelling type, either all IPv4 or all IPv6. The border routers neither maintain nor distribute the VPN-IPv6 routes and need not carry both IP versions: each keeps labelled IPv4 or IPv6 routes to the provider edge routers inside its own autonomous system and passes them on with external BGP, which builds a label switched path from the ingress to the egress provider edge router. Provider edge routers in different autonomous systems can then set up multihop external BGP connections to each other over IPv4 or IPv6 and exchange the labelled VPN-IPv6 routes over them. The route reflectors, the third label and the label switched paths spanning several autonomous systems, all discussed for the IPv4 case in RFC 4364, apply equally here.

Several other cases follow the IPv4 rules. An IPv6 VPN may be the network of an IPv6 internet service provider with its own peering and routing policy, or the network of a provider that sells VPN service to its own customers, and it may buy backbone service from another provider using the carriers' carrier method of RFC 4364, applied to IPv6 traffic. Access to the global IPv6 internet from an IPv6 VPN uses the methods of RFC 4364, but if the packets have to cross an IPv4-only backbone they must be tunnelled through it, and access to the internet needs global IPv6 addresses, so unique local addresses cannot be used for it. For management, the considerations of RFC 4364 apply, and where the provider manages the customer router over IPv4, that router is effectively part of an IPv4 VPN as well as the IPv6 one, so the measures that keep management traffic between different VPNs apart apply to the IPv4 side of its VRF.
sections.plainLanguage: When the sites of one private network sit in different provider networks, there are three ways to connect them: exchange plain IPv6 routes between the border routers, pass the labelled private routes from one network to the next, or build a label switched path across several networks and pass the private routes over it. The other cases, such as a provider buying backbone service from another provider or customers reaching the internet, follow the same rules as the IPv4 service.

sections.title: Security, Quality of Service and Scale
sections.content:
The extensions in this document let multiprotocol BGP propagate reachability information about IPv6 VPN routes. The security considerations for carrying IPv6 reachability information over BGP, discussed in Section 5 of RFC 2545, apply just as they do to the extensions described here. The IPv6 VPN service is offered with exactly the same approach as the IPv4 service of RFC 4364, so the same security considerations apply for data plane security, control plane security, and the security of the provider edge and provider devices.

The quality of service mechanisms that RFC 4364 describes for IPv4 VPNs operate in the same way for IPv4 and IPv6, covering Diffserv, Intserv and MPLS traffic engineering. The same considerations therefore apply to IPv6 VPNs, and they hold whether the backbone uses IPv4 tunnelling or IPv6 tunnelling.

Each scalability consideration summarised for IPv4 VPNs in RFC 4364 is equally applicable to IPv6 VPNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules of its own, because the IPv6 service works the same way as the IPv4 one, so the same protections and the same limits on scale apply. The same is true of quality of service: the mechanisms that give a customer a guaranteed service behave the same whichever IP version the backbone uses.
